entry.title: Learn to Play the Easiest 90's Riff — Santa Monica by Everclear

media:group.media:title: Learn to Play the Easiest 90's Riff — Santa Monica by Everclear
media:group.media:description:
Santa Monica by Everclear is one of those riffs that sounds instantly familiar and takes about two minutes to learn. Start with a G power chord, then just lift your index finger off to let the open low E ring in. That's the whole move.
It's a great early win if you're newer to guitar, and it's the kind of riff that actually sounds like a song from the first time you play it. Sometimes that's exactly what you need to keep the momentum going.
Go have fun with that one!

entry.title: Learn JANE SAYS by Jane's Addiction Right Now

media:group.media:title: Learn JANE SAYS by Jane's Addiction Right Now
media:group.media:description:
Jane Says by Jane's Addiction is one of those riffs that sounds instantly recognizable and feels great to play. It's just two chords, G and A, but the way the A chord is voiced is what gives it that loose, percussive quality.
Instead of a full A chord, you're using the one-finger version and adding pull-offs on the G and D strings. That little release after each hit is what makes the riff breathe and groove the way it does. Simple idea, a lot of feel.
Great one for beginners and a fun one to just sit and strum along to.

entry.title: 5 Legendary Songs You Can Play With Only 2 Easy Chords • Beatles, Springsteen & More

media:group.media:title: 5 Legendary Songs You Can Play With Only 2 Easy Chords • Beatles, Springsteen & More
media:group.media:description:
Some of the most legendary songs ever written are built on just two easy chords. In this guitar lesson I break down five of them, and most are variations on that one-four relationship that just feels so good.
We’ll also talk a little about the one-four relationship, Dorian and Mixolydian sounds, and how these simple progressions can give you a great foundation for jamming and improvising.
The 5 songs: Born in the U.S.A. (Bruce Springsteen) — B to E Oye Como Va (Santana) — A minor 7 to D7, pure Dorian Fire on the Mountain (Grateful Dead) — B to A, B Mixolydian Feelin' Alright (Joe Cocker) — C7 to F7 with one moveable shape Paperback Writer (The Beatles) — G to C
The big takeaway: you really don’t need a ton of chords to make great music.

entry.title: The Easiest Way to Play Over Blues Changes

media:group.media:title: The Easiest Way to Play Over Blues Changes
media:group.media:description:
One of the coolest things about playing blues in E is that the three chords, E7, A7, and B7, each have a distinct note on the G string that tells you exactly where you are in the progression. First fret for E7, open G for A7, second fret for B7. Just three reference points and suddenly the changes start to make sense under your fingers.
The idea is to stay in your pentatonic or blues scale like normal, but let that one note on the G string anchor you to whichever chord is happening. You start hearing the changes rather than just hoping your licks fit.
It's a really approachable entry point into playing over changes instead of just playing over a static key. Mess around with that!

entry.title: Stop Playing the Same D, G, and A — Try These Inversions

media:group.media:title: Stop Playing the Same D, G, and A — Try These Inversions
media:group.media:description:
Playing a 1, 4, 5 progression the same way every time gets the job done, but having alternate voicings for each chord gives you so much more to work with. These aren't better or worse than the open chord versions, just different colors that keep the ear interested.
For D, G, and A I'm pulling voicings from the CAGED system but only using the top three strings on each one, which keeps things clean and avoids any heavy barre chord work. The notes move in a completely different direction compared to the standard voicings, and that movement is what makes a simple progression feel more alive.
The more options you have for any given chord, the more you can shape a progression into something that actually goes somewhere. Try it out!

media:group.media:title: Playing The Black Crowes Live at East Iris Studios: Jealous Again
media:group.media:description:
One of my favorite things about making all these guitar lessons is getting the chance to actually get in a room with great musicians and PLAY.
Here's the Marty Music Trio performing The Black Crowes "Jealous Again" live at East Iris Studios in Nashville.
Marty Music Trio: Dylan Zangwill — organ & vocals Dekar Justus — drums Marty Schwartz — guitar
Recorded Live at East Iris Studios in Nashville, TN. Mixed by Lewin Barringer @GaragebandandBeyond
There's something about that Crowes sound. The organ, the swagger, the way it just breathes. We had a blast with this one. Turn it up!
